p-nungwi-landing.name: Nungwi landing
p-nungwi-landing.teaser: Kingfish, tuna and octopus come off the ngalawa and the mashua and are sold by the kilo on the sand
p-nungwi-landing.story: There is no fixed hour here: the boats come in when the tide lets them, and the auction happens wherever they ground. So the first thing you buy at Nungwi is information. Ask on your first morning when the boats go out tomorrow, then be on the sand when they come back. Bring cash in small notes, agree the price per kilo before anything is weighed or cut, and buy your ice in the same place in the same minute. Octopus is cheapest around the spring tides, when the flats give it up; the kingfish you want whole, for the grill.
p-nungwi-landing.why: Buy at the boat, not later: the fish has never been fresher or cheaper than at the moment it hits the sand.
facts: Every day the boats go out
Timed by the tide, so the landing moves later by roughly fifty minutes a day
Whatever hour the fishermen tell you the day before
Nguru (kingfish) to grill whole, jodari (tuna) raw or seared, pweza (octopus) around spring tides, ngisi (squid) if you cook it fast, kamba (prawn and lobster) when there is any
Cash in small shillings, price per kilo agreed before the knife

p-mkokotoni.name: Mkokotoni
p-mkokotoni.teaser: A shouted auction where the town's fish shops buy, over before most hotels have cleared breakfast
p-mkokotoni.story: Nungwi is a beach negotiation; Mkokotoni is a market. The district's landing is where the fish shops buy, so the range is wider, the prices are the ones professionals pay and the bidding is shouted rather than smiled. It is worth the drive only if you are buying seriously, and only if you are early: anything big or unusual goes in the first sale, and the slab is bare by mid-morning. Stand where the buyers stand, watch one lot go before you bid, and have your shillings ready in small notes.
p-mkokotoni.why: Be there before the first sale; that is when the large and the unusual fish are still on the slab.
facts: From early morning, finished by mid-morning
More range and better prices than Nungwi, and the big fish before the town buyers take them

p-dukas.name: Nungwi village dukas
p-dukas.teaser: A hundred small shops, rice by the kilo, island bananas, and not one block of cheese at the north tip
p-dukas.story: There is no proper supermarket at the north tip. What there is: a line of dukas through the village, each a doorway and a counter, selling rice, wheat flour, cooking oil, UHT milk, eggs, onions, tomatoes, limes, chillies, salt, sugar, tea and charcoal. Fruit sellers set up beside them with mango, papaya, passion fruit, pineapple and the small sweet island bananas, and fresh coconut for grating. Cook simply and you will want for nothing. Cook as you do at home and you will notice what is missing within a day.
p-dukas.why: Plan your menu around what the dukas carry and the landing brings in; everything else is a Stone Town run.
facts: Daily, except around Friday midday when the village closes for prayers
Morning, before the heat and with the fruit fresh
Rice, flour, oil, eggs, limes, chillies, charcoal, island bananas, passion fruit, coconut
Butter, cheese, wine, cream, good coffee beans, fresh herbs, or reliably chilled anything

p-darajani.name: Darajani, for the deep inventory
p-darajani.teaser: Cloves and cardamom by the scoop, at a fraction of what the same spice costs in a printed gift box
p-darajani.story: Stone Town's market is the deepest inventory on the island, and it is where the spice trade turns back into shopping. Spice is sold loose, by the scoop and by weight: cloves, cardamom, cinnamon bark and leaf, nutmeg still in its mace, black pepper, vanilla, tamarind, and dried dagaa for the stock pot. Smell everything before you pay. The fish hall at the back is finished by late morning. And this is the day to fill the bag with what the north tip does not have: Stone Town's supermarkets carry the cheese, butter, wine and coffee.
p-darajani.why: Buy your spice loose and by weight here, never boxed, and smell it first.
facts: From dawn; the fish hall runs about 07:00 to 10:00
First thing, while the fish hall is still going
Cloves, cardamom, cinnamon bark and leaf, nutmeg with mace, black pepper, vanilla, tamarind, dried dagaa
Stone Town's supermarkets for the cheese, butter, wine and coffee you cannot get up north

p-ice.name: Ice is the bottleneck
p-ice.teaser: The power goes, the fridge goes with it, so the shopping trip on this cape is a daily event, not a weekly one
p-ice.story: Power cuts are routine at the north tip and generators are not universal, so assume nothing you buy will survive to tomorrow. Buy ice at the landing in the same minute you buy the fish, keep it in a shaded cool box, and build the day's menu around what came home with you. That is how the whole island eats. The other rule is older: drink bottled or properly filtered water, rinse salad and anything raw in it, and buy it in large refill containers rather than a stream of small bottles. The plastic on the beaches is why.
p-ice.why: Cook what you bought that morning, the same day, and nothing goes wrong.
facts: Buy ice with the fish, keep it in a shaded cool box, cook the same day
Count on a fridge overnight; power cuts are routine
Bottled or filtered for drinking and for rinsing anything eaten raw; large refill containers from the village dukas
Cooked through or peeled; the market grills are fine because everything goes over live coals in front of you

p-coconut.name: Learn the coconut
p-coconut.teaser: One coconut, two milks: the thin one simmers with the onions, the thick one goes in last or the sauce splits
p-coconut.story: Fresh coconut is everywhere and it is the base of nearly everything cooked here. Grate the flesh on a mbuzi, the grating stool, and press it twice. The first press gives a thick milk; water through the same gratings gives a thin second one. The thin goes in early, to cook down with the onion and spice. The thick goes in at the end, off a hard boil, or it splits badly rather than well. Get that order right and mchuzi wa nazi, the island's coconut fish curry, comes out of your own kitchen tasting like the village's.
p-coconut.why: The thick milk goes in last and never boils; that one rule is the difference.
facts: Thin milk early with the aromatics, thick milk at the end off the boil
Fresh coconuts from the village fruit sellers; the mbuzi stool at a village hardware duka
Mchuzi wa nazi, coconut fish curry

p-shillings.name: Buy in shillings, ask in Kiswahili
p-shillings.teaser: Two words, bei gani, change what you are shown at a slab and what you end up paying for it
p-shillings.story: Dollars are welcome in hotels and a liability in a market: they mark you as a hotel guest before you have opened your mouth. Carry Tanzanian shillings in small notes, so nobody has to find change for a large one. Then use the words. Bei gani? How much. Kwa kilo: per kilo. Asante: thank you. Settle the price per kilo before anything is weighed, cut or put on a fire, and the conversation stays friendly. For the names of the fish themselves, the sea stories have the name ladder.
p-shillings.why: Settle the price per kilo before anything is weighed, cut or lit.
facts: Bei gani? (how much) · Kwa kilo (per kilo) · Asante (thank you)
Pay in dollars at a market; cards are for hotels only

f-highland.name: Highland Bungalows
f-highland.teaser: Pool tables, the football on, chapati wraps, and the only lights still on inland when the beach has gone dark
f-highland.story: When the beach bars have stacked their chairs, this is where the north tip carries on. Highland is the local bar inland: pool tables, the football on the screen, cheap drinks and a kitchen that does chapati wraps and stir-fried noodles. It is not good food and does not pretend to be. It is good company, at about a third of the beach price, later than anywhere else, and the room is not arranged for visitors, which is the point of it.
f-highland.why: Go for the company and the hour, not the plate.
facts: Chapati wraps, stir-fried noodles, a cheap beer
Late, after everything else has shut
About a third of the beach price
A torch; the way is inland and unlit, so walk back with somebody

f-che-rock.name: Che Rock, up to 23:00
f-che-rock.teaser: The kitchen runs to eleven, which up here counts as late, and the strip's own staff eat at the next table
f-che-rock.story: At the main entrance to Nungwi beach, beside Pasha Nungwi, Che Rock serves tacos, burgers and pub plates until eleven at night. That alone would make it useful on this coast. What makes it reliable is who is eating: this is where the strip's own bar and dive staff come on their night off, so the kitchen stays honest right up to the bell. Come off a late dive or a long sunset, sit down with a burger and a cocktail, among the people who work the strip.
f-che-rock.why: Get your order in by half past ten and the kitchen will still be cooking properly.
facts: A burger or tacos, and a cocktail
Main beach entrance, beside Pasha Nungwi

f-chipsi.name: Chipsi mayai, from a cart
f-chipsi.teaser: Chips folded into beaten egg and set in a pan: Tanzania's own answer to two in the morning
f-chipsi.story: Chipsi mayai is chips and eggs, literally, and it is cooked across the whole country from small kitchens and carts. Fries go into a pan, beaten egg goes over them, and it sets like a frittata. It is far better than it sounds when the egg is only just set and the chips are still crisp at the edges. Up here it is the after-the-bar food, such as it is, and on the nights the village carts are out it is the only thing being cooked at that hour.
f-chipsi.why: Ask for it with the egg barely set; that is when it is good.
facts: Village kitchens and carts, and the market end of the beach
After the bars, on nights the carts are out

f-closes-early.name: This coast closes early
f-closes-early.teaser: Kitchens stop between ten and eleven, and Kendwa's one club opens at ten, after every one of them has shut
f-closes-early.story: Except on club nights and the monthly full moon, Nungwi is quiet before midnight and Kendwa quieter still. Kitchens stop between about 22:00 and 23:00, and anything you order after that is luck. The trap is Kendwa Rocks' club, The Rocks Lounge: it opens at 22:00, by which time nothing in Kendwa is cooking. Eat first or eat at breakfast. And settle the ride home before the first drink, because the beach walk between the villages is shut at high water and unwise after dark in any case.
f-closes-early.why: Eat before ten, and book the taxi back before you start drinking.
facts: The Rocks Lounge from 22:00 on its three nights · Maisha Beach Fri and Sat from 20:00
Rocks Lounge entry around 25,000 TZS on a club night; taxi Kendwa–Nungwi about 20,000 TZS each way (seen Aug 2026)
Walk the beach between the villages at night

f-ramadan.name: And in Ramadan it inverts
f-ramadan.teaser: The village that shuts at ten in August is still eating at eleven, because in Ramadan the day starts at sunset
f-ramadan.story: During Ramadan, Zanzibar requires restaurants, bars and food outlets outside hotel compounds to close through the daylight hours across the archipelago, and to reopen after sunset for iftar. Hotels keep serving, but for registered guests and in designated areas only, and alcohol is restricted more generally, often served only after iftar. Then the evenings take over. They run long and busy in a way the rest of the calendar never does: the one time of year this island genuinely eats late. Plan the days quietly and the nights properly.
f-ramadan.why: Save your appetite for after sunset; Ramadan evenings are the best eating of the year.
facts: Eat at your hotel by day; go out after iftar
Eat, drink or smoke in public during fasting hours; wear beachwear beyond the beach and hotel grounds
Your hotel when its bar serves; often only after iftar
The Ramadan dates against your travel dates before booking

m-1996.name: 1996, on a clear full moon
m-1996.teaser: A few friends, some guests, fires on the sand and drumming till dawn: then thirty years, and thousands
m-1996.story: By Kendwa Rocks' own account, the Full Moon Party began in 1996 on a clear full-moon night with a group of friends and a few guests: fires on the sand, acrobats, drums through the night. The hotel still tells it that way. What it grew into is the other half. Thirty years on it runs every month, with international DJs, fire shows, dancers and a buffet that spans Zanzibari, Indian, Arabic, Thai and Indonesian cooking, and it draws thousands. Neither description is false. They are two different nights wearing the same name, and the beach under both is the same sand.
m-1996.why: The beach-fire night and the festival are the same event thirty years apart; know which one you are walking into.
facts: The party, monthly, on the sand in front of Kendwa Rocks
The 1996 date and the founding scene rest on the venue's own telling

m-when.name: When it happens
m-when.teaser: Not on the full moon: on the Saturday after it, and people miss it by five days every month
m-when.story: The party runs on the first Saturday after each full moon, not on the full moon itself. That catches more visitors than anything else on this beach: people book a week around the lunar date and miss it by five days, or book what they think is a quiet week and land in the middle of it. It starts at sunset and the buffet opens around seven; the music runs late. Some third-party listings put it on the Saturday nearest the full moon, so take the date from the venue's own calendar before you book a room; the coming months are on the hot board.
m-when.why: Read the venue's calendar before the booking site; room prices that weekend are not the week before's.
facts: First Saturday after each full moon, by the venue's account (seen Aug 2026); from sunset, buffet around 19:00
Confirm the date on the venue's calendar; some listings say the Saturday nearest the full moon

sources.label: We Are Zanzibar: Full Moon Party at Kendwa Rocks

m-rest.name: The rest of the month
m-rest.teaser: Twenty-nine nights a month the famous address is a beach bar with a cold beer and the best sand in Kendwa
m-rest.story: Away from that one Saturday, Kendwa Rocks is a straightforward beach hotel: a kitchen, a bar, and a cheap sundowner on the best-positioned sand in the village. The famous name does not show on an ordinary evening. Its club, The Rocks Lounge, opens Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday nights, and on the others the loudest thing is the sea. If either bar is busy, Sunset Kendwa, fifty metres up the beach, is the quieter choice on any night.
m-rest.why: Come on an ordinary night for the sunset and the sand, at an ordinary price.
facts: Bar and kitchen through the day; The Rocks Lounge Tue, Thu and Sat
Kendwa Rocks, centre of Kendwa sand
Sunset Kendwa, fifty metres up the beach, when it is crowded

m-want.name: If you want it
m-want.teaser: The whole cape fills that weekend, not just the hotel, and the morning after is a Muslim fishing village
m-want.story: Book the room months ahead, because the whole village fills, not only the venue, and buy the ticket in advance. Eat properly somewhere else first: a buffet feeding thousands is a buffet feeding thousands. Arrange the ride home before you start. Then hold one thing in mind. The party happens on the western edge of a conservative Muslim village whose people mostly do not attend it, though it is a real part of the local economy. What is normal on the sand at two in the morning is not normal on the road at nine.
m-want.why: Cover up, keep it quiet and carry no open bottle once you leave the sand.
facts: Room months ahead; ticket in advance
Around 50,000 TZS for the Full Moon Party (seen Aug 2026)
Eat beforehand elsewhere; fix the ride home first
Walk into the village loud, uncovered or with an open bottle

m-dont.name: If you don't
m-dont.teaser: The noise carries a few hundred metres: walk twenty minutes, or turn one corner of the cape, and it is gone
m-dont.story: The noise is local to a few hundred metres of Kendwa sand, and you can escape it in steps. Walk twenty minutes north to the Kilindi end of the beach. Go three kilometres to the Nungwi strip, which runs its own quieter Saturday, with Maisha Beach's Sunset Saxophone Session. Or go round the point to the east-facing bay behind it, near Essque Zalu, out of earshot completely. Simplest of all: pick a week that does not straddle the Saturday after a full moon. The tide table and the moon phase are the two documents that plan a week here.
m-dont.why: Check the moon before you book, and the problem never arises.
facts: The Kilindi end · the Nungwi strip · the east-facing bay behind the point
Choose dates clear of the Saturday after the full moon

o-mkokotoni.name: Mkokotoni
o-mkokotoni.teaser: The district capital, twenty kilometres south: no tourism, a fish auction, and Tumbatu just offshore
o-mkokotoni.story: Twenty kilometres south of Kendwa the west-coast road reaches Mkokotoni, the regional capital of Unguja North, and the tourist economy simply stops. It is a working town: the landing that supplies the fish shops, a shouted morning auction, and the jetty for Tumbatu, the island directly offshore, whose boats come across with their catch. You go early, see the sale, watch the Watumbatu boats in, and are back at the beach for lunch. Bring cash and go as a buyer rather than a spectator.
o-mkokotoni.why: Watch the Tumbatu boats come in to the jetty while the auction is still shouting.
facts: About 20 km south on the west-coast road, 30 minutes each way
The jetty, with the Tumbatu boats landing

o-kizimbani.name: Kizimbani spice plantation
o-kizimbani.teaser: Pick a cinnamon leaf and smell it: it smells of clove, and that surprise is the whole lesson
o-kizimbani.story: Kizimbani is one of the oldest of the island's spice estates, inland from Stone Town on the road you will drive anyway, and the one to choose if you want agriculture rather than a gift shop. You see cloves picked and dried, vanilla climbing its vines, nutmeg in its red mace, cinnamon as bark and as leaf. Harvest activity peaks in the dry windows, June to October and December to February. One warning: every driver on this island has a spice farm he is paid to take you to. Name Kizimbani when you book, and hold to it.
o-kizimbani.why: Insist on Kizimbani by name, and ask to crush a cinnamon leaf.
facts: Inland from Stone Town on the road from Kendwa; arrange the car the day before
Half a day including the transfer
June to October and December to February, the dry-window harvests
Cloves drying, nutmeg with mace, the clove-scented cinnamon leaf

o-mangapwani.name: Mangapwani
o-mangapwani.teaser: A coral cave with a freshwater spring, and a kilometre away, a cell cut in stone and used until about 1905
o-mangapwani.story: Two sites a kilometre apart on the west-coast road, about twenty kilometres north of Stone Town. The coral cave is natural, with a freshwater spring inside, which is why it could hide people. The chamber is man-made, cut around 1880 by Mohammed bin Nassor Al-Alwi, and it held human cargo until about 1905, more than thirty years after the 1873 treaty that was supposed to end the trade. You go down the steps into it. This is the other half of the spice story, and it does not fit into a light half hour between beaches.
o-mangapwani.why: Take a guide who will tell it properly; it is the honest counterweight to every spice tour.
facts: On the west-coast road between Kendwa and Stone Town; stop on the Stone Town drive
Around US$5 a foreign adult (seen Aug 2026)
The steps down into the chamber

o-stone-town.name: Stone Town, done in one day
o-stone-town.teaser: Market at dawn, memorial by mid-morning, carved doors at noon, and the Forodhani grills lighting at six
o-stone-town.story: Stone Town, UNESCO-listed in 2000, is the port that assembled everything you eat at the north tip, and it will not fit into an afternoon. The day that works: leave Kendwa by eight, reach Darajani while the fish hall is still going, then Christ Church and the slave-market memorial. Lunch at Lukmaan's counter. Lose the hot hours in the alleys among the carved doors, reach the Old Fort at five, and walk the seafront past the closed House of Wonders to Forodhani Gardens, laid out in 1936 for the sultan's jubilee and rebuilt in 2009 by the Aga Khan Trust, as the grills light around six.
o-stone-town.why: End at Forodhani at dusk, and eat only what is cooked in front of you.
facts: 56 km, about 1 h 15 each way; private car roughly US$50–70 each way, shared transfers less (seen Aug 2026); arrange the day before
Christ Church and the slave-market memorial; Forodhani stalls from about 18:00 to 21:00
Lunch at Lukmaan; Forodhani at dusk, cash only, price it before it is made

o-the-roof.name: …or stay the night for the roof
o-the-roof.teaser: One sitting a night on a roof above the old town, with the call to prayer rising from four directions
o-the-roof.story: The argument for a night in Stone Town is a roof. At the Emerson Spice Tea House the sundowners start at six and the first course of a seafood tasting menu arrives at seven, one sitting, while the call to prayer comes up from four directions and the light goes over the sea. Its sister roof, Emerson on Hurumzi, seats you on rugs for three courses with live taarab, the island's own orchestral song. It is the best dinner on the island, and you cannot have it and drive back to Kendwa the same night.
o-the-roof.why: Book a roof and a bed: the dinner and the drive north do not fit in one evening.
facts: Seafood tasting menu US$55, one sitting; sundowners from 18:00, first course 19:00 (seen Aug 2026)
Three courses US$45, live taarab, floor seating on rugs; deposit required (seen Aug 2026)
Both in advance; confirm the day, as the rooftops have carried scheduled closures

g-work-truth.name: Do not plan to work here
g-work-truth.teaser: Power cuts, mobile data, salt air and glare: a beautiful place to close the laptop
g-work-truth.story: There is no co-working infrastructure at the north tip. Power cuts are routine and generators are not universal. Connectivity in practice means mobile data, which is cheap and fine for mail and messages and not for anything heavy. Add glare that defeats most screens, sand in every hinge and salt air that kills keyboards, and the honest advice is to bring a book, not a deliverable. If you genuinely must work, do it early from your own room, and be finished by ten.
g-work-truth.why: Bring a book, not a deliverable.
facts: Buy a local SIM with data at the airport; work early, from your room
Rely on hotel wifi or a beach table for a call
Finish by ten and go in the water
